messages.author: 7f7355d1143e7e9f
messages.subject: forecast a disease risk using a dynamic model
parts:
Hi everyone, 

I want to forecast disease risk using the INLA package. Let me introduce my data first. Parasitological data, including number of infected individuals and population at risk, are available in a province from 1997 to 2010 at the county level (i.e., polygon data in county) as well as some risk factors (e.g., temperature, rainfall, and wetness). I want to forecast the disease risk, that's the risks in 2011,2012, and etc. 

I've tried the LINA package in R recently. It can take into account the spatial correlation and count data, but it seems that it can only smooth the data using the historical data, it cannot forecast.  I have read some references written by  Ramiro Ruiz-Cardenas (e.g., Fitting dynamic models using integrated nested Laplace approximations - INLA), but no example is related to forecast. Dose anyone could help me out? thank you so much!

Regards

Yi

Hi,

you have to build the forcast into your model, using NA as the response.
see the FAQ entry on this topic and the FAQ entry on the use of 'NA'.

the following example shows how

Best
H

********************************************

n = 100
npred = 30
N = n + npred
eta = arima.sim(n=n, model = list(ar = 0.9))
eta = scale(eta)
y = eta + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)

yy = c(y, rep(NA, npred))
idx = 1:N

r = inla(yy ~ 1 + f(idx, model="ar1"),
data = data.frame(yy, idx),
control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))

plot(idx, r$summary.linear.predictor$mean, type="l", lwd=2)
lines(idx, r$summary.linear.predictor$"0.025quant", col="red", lwd=2)
lines(idx, r$summary.linear.predictor$"0.975quant", col="red", lwd=2)

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] forecast a disease risk using a dynamic model
parts:
On 30/05/15 09:20, Håvard Rue wrote:
> you have to build the forcast into your model, using NA as the response.

There is an example in the material I used for a recent INLA course at
http://www.math.ntnu.no/~eliask/br2015/
The file r/cwb-select.R runs 864 models including 5 (five) space-time
models type. The forecast is done for one year ahead (the outcome for
2009 is set as NA in the example) and one year before (there is no
outcome observed for 1995).

In other work I and a colleague tried to evaluate models for 2 steps
ahead. Our experience is that random effects (like dynamic intercepts)
are not good to forecast as to fit the data. In the example above you
can see that the best models for forecast (low mse) includes parametric
trends instead of complex random effects and the better fitting (low DIC
and LCPO) includes complex random effects.

Elias

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] forecast a disease risk using a dynamic model
parts:
On 31/05/15 04:55, 胡艺 wrote:
> I'm wondering what we can forecast in 2010, using the best predictive
> model, the number of death (if this is the case, there is no expected
> number of death available, right?) or the SMR?

In the example we have the model
y_t ~ Poisson(\lambda_t)
\lambda_t = E_t R_t = E(y_t)
where R_t is the fitted SMR for time t.

To predict \lambda_t+1 = E(y_t+1) you need some guess for the population
at risk in 2010 to compute E_t+1. However, R_t+1 can be predicted
considering E_t+1=1

n <- 15
E <- rgamma(n, 10, 1)

x <- log(3-1:n/n+0.03*(1:n)^2/n)

y <- rpois(n, exp(1 + x))
plot(x)

require(INLA)

r <- inla(y ~ f(i, model='rw1'), 'poisson', E=c(E0, 1),
data=list(y=c(y,NA), i=c(1:n,n+1)),
control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1))
r$summary.fitted[n+(-1:1),]

Elias
